definition: Knell means the solemn sound of a bell, often indicating a death.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word knell. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know knell should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The convent bell rang a slow knell at dawn, and the town understood that the eldest sister had died in the night.
A chime is far lighter than a knell — a bright note marking the hour or a visitor at the door.
A toll is milder than a knell — bells toll slowly for many solemn occasions, but a knell announces a death or an ending.

A harbinger is an early sign that something is on its way — the first frost, a swallow before summer. It is a sign, not a sound, and what it points to may be good or bad. A knell is heard, and it announces only endings.

An alarm is rung to warn — fire, flood, wake up — urgent, fast, and aimed at what is still coming, so that people can act. A knell is the opposite tempo: slow and solemn, sounded when the ending has already arrived and nothing can be done.

Knell stands alone in modern English: its parent verb cnyllan died out, leaving no cousins to recognize. What survives instead is the phrase it anchors — the 'death knell' — which lets one Old English syllable go on announcing endings a millennium later.
Knell means the solemn sound of a bell, often indicating a death.

When the council voted to close the village school, the chairman said he heard a knell in the word 'carried': a village that loses its school, he told the room, has heard the first bell of its own funeral.
A knell is not just any ringing — it is the slow, solemn bell that announces a death, and by extension any signal that something is finished.
That is why English speaks of a 'death knell' for trades, laws, and eras.
Knell is the bell that announces a death — and, figuratively, any signal that something is over: the ruling sounded the knell for the old law.
Chimes are neutral and peals are joyful; a knell only ever means an ending.
Its unit-mate dirge is the song sung after the news; the knell is the bell that breaks it.

In the village where my grandfather grew up, the church bell had two voices.
Quick, bright ringing meant weddings, victories, the end of a war.
But a slow, single stroke repeated at long intervals meant only one thing, and every kitchen fell silent to count.
That sound was the knell, and it was never rung in warning.
By the time it spoke, whatever it spoke of was already over.
Grandfather said you could tell how the village aged by which voice you heard more often.
When the parish finally closed the church, no one rang anything at all — and he said the silence that day was the heaviest stroke of all.
